lines.text: A thousand years of kings and plagues, Vikings and crusaders, and the great cities of the Maya, Aztecs and Incas. This is the world of the Middle Ages.
Our story starts far back in the Andes, where people kept records on knotted cords. The Inca would later run an empire with them.
In Mexico and Central America, the Maya rose as a world of rival city-states, with stepped pyramids, glyphs and an exact calendar.
On the Gulf coast, the Olmecs carved colossal stone heads and built the first great ceremonial centres, a mother culture for those who followed.
In the valleys of Oaxaca, the Zapotecs levelled a mountaintop for their city of Monte Alban, and wrote with an early script of their own.
Far to the south, the Nazca people scratched giant animals and lines into the Peruvian desert, figures best seen from the sky.
The Maya counted time in linked cycles: a sacred count of two hundred and sixty days, a solar year, and the Long Count for the ages.
Deep in the rainforest of Guatemala, Tikal grew into one of the greatest Maya cities, its temples rising above the trees.
The Maya wrote too, carving signs for words and syllables on monuments and in folding books, a script only read again in our own time.
Near today's Mexico City, a vast planned city rose around the Pyramids of the Sun and Moon. Its builders are unknown; the Aztecs gave it its name.
Meanwhile in northern Europe, Germanic peoples carved runes into wood, stone and metal, letters the Vikings would one day raise on memorial stones.
In the forests of southern Mexico, the Maya city of Palenque left carved texts that tell much of what we know of Maya history.
As Rome fell in the west, its eastern half lived on from Constantinople, keeping Greek learning and Roman law alive for a thousand years.
In Scandinavia people honoured Odin, Thor and Freya, and told of a final battle called Ragnarok.
So begins the age historians call the Middle Ages, between the fall of the western empire and the Renaissance, an age of lords, monks and cathedrals.
A humble invention changed the fields: the padded horse collar, which let horses pull heavy ploughs without choking, and slowly replace the ox.
In the Yucatan, Chichen Itza grew into a centre of trade and ritual, with its great stepped pyramid and its ball court.
In Italy, Saint Benedict wrote a rule for monks. Benedictine monasteries would copy manuscripts and keep learning alive across Europe.
At Palenque, Pakal took the throne at twelve and reigned for almost seventy years, building temples and a tomb found again in 1952.
In 732, Charles Martel and the Franks turned back an Umayyad army in France, a battle that became a lasting symbol in European history.
His grandson Charlemagne conquered much of western Europe and was crowned emperor by the Pope on Christmas Day in the year 800.
Then came the Viking Age, when Norse seafarers raided, traded and settled from the British Isles to Iceland, Greenland and beyond.
It opened with terror in 793, when raiders fell on the monastery of Lindisfarne off north-east England, killing monks and seizing its treasures.
Their weapon was the longship, narrow and shallow, able to cross open sea and slip up rivers deep into the land.
Across the ocean, many Maya cities of the southern lowlands emptied, worn down by drought, war and political breakdown. The Maya people remained.
In 843, Charlemagne's three grandsons split his empire between them, and its western and eastern parts began to become France and Germany.
In England, Alfred of Wessex held the Vikings back when other kingdoms fell, and built a navy, made laws and championed English learning.
To the east, Slavic princedoms gathered around Kyiv. Their ruler Vladimir took Orthodox Christianity, and Kievan Rus' took shape.
In central Mexico the Toltecs flourished at Tula, remembered by the later Aztecs as master builders and artists.
The Wessex kings now joined the English into one kingdom, a monarchy that would last for almost eight centuries.
In Iceland, around 930, chieftains met in the open air at the Althing to recite the law, often called the oldest parliament still meeting.
Erik the Red, outlawed from Iceland, sailed west and founded the first Norse settlements in Greenland.
In 962, Otto the First was crowned emperor, beginning the Holy Roman Empire, a loose union of German and Italian lands that lasted eight hundred years.
Erik's son Leif sailed further still, and around the year 1000 reached a land he called Vinland, in North America.
Cnut, a Danish prince, took the English crown in 1016 and ruled Denmark and Norway too, an empire around the North Sea.
On the tip of Newfoundland, the remains of Norse turf houses prove the sagas right: Europeans stood in America five centuries before Columbus.
Harald Hardrada, once a guard of the Byzantine emperor, became king of Norway and set his sights on England.
Across the Channel, William, Duke of Normandy, was waiting with a claim of his own.
William began a fortress beside the Thames, the Tower of London, to hold the city he had won.
In the autumn of 1066, King Harold defeated Hardrada at Stamford Bridge, then raced south to meet the Normans. The Viking Age was ending.
At Hastings, Harold fell and William was crowned. Norman rule would change England's law, language and lords for good.
The story was stitched into the Bayeux Tapestry, about seventy metres of embroidered pictures ending with the battle itself.
To learn what his kingdom held, William ordered a great survey of land and property, so final that people called it the Domesday Book.
In Bologna, students gathered to study law, founding what is seen as the oldest university in the Western world.
In 1096, Pope Urban the Second called Christians east. Three years later, the crusaders took Jerusalem.
They founded the Kingdom of Jerusalem, a Crusader state that would cling to the coast of the Holy Land for almost two centuries.
High in the Andes, Cusco was growing into the city that would become the capital of the Incas.
Warrior monks, the Knights Templar, swore to guard pilgrims. They grew rich through gifts and banking, until a French king turned on them.
Eleanor of Aquitaine ruled lands in her own right, married the kings of France and then England, and was mother to two English kings.
Saladin, ruler of Egypt and Syria, united Muslim lands against the crusaders, and in 1187 took Jerusalem back.
In Paris, a university grew into Europe's leading school of theology, its students speaking Latin in what is still the Latin Quarter.
Richard the Lionheart, king of England, spent most of his reign abroad, fighting for the Holy Land.
In Syria, the Knights Hospitaller held Krak des Chevaliers, a castle of double walls and sloping towers, among the strongest of its age.
In Italy, Francis of Assisi gave up a rich family's wealth to live in poverty, and founded the Franciscan friars.
Richard led the Third Crusade with the king of France. It won back coastal cities, but not Jerusalem, and ended in a truce with Saladin.
In the Andes the Incas worshipped Inti, the sun, along with mountains, springs and their ancestors' mummies. Their emperor was a child of the sun.
In 1215, English barons forced King John to seal Magna Carta at Runnymede: even a king, it said, was bound by the law.
At Chartres, a Gothic cathedral rose after a fire, its stained glass glowing through the centuries and shaping churches to come.
Thomas Aquinas joined the thought of Aristotle to Christian teaching, becoming one of the great minds of the medieval Church.
Around the Baltic and North Seas, merchant towns led by Lubeck banded together as the Hanseatic League to protect their trade.
In Florence, Dante Alighieri was born, the poet who would write in Italian rather than Latin.
In Iceland, the old poems of gods, giants and heroes were written down in the Poetic Edda, our main window on Norse myth.
Dante's Divine Comedy took readers through Hell, Purgatory and Paradise, and made Tuscan the basis of the Italian language.
In 1325, the Mexica founded Tenochtitlan on an island in Lake Texcoco, linked to the shore by causeways.
Their gods, Huitzilopochtli and Tlaloc among them, demanded offerings, including human sacrifice, to keep the sun moving across the sky.
At the heart of the city stood the Templo Mayor, with twin shrines on its summit. Its ruins lay hidden under Mexico City until 1978.
In 1337, England and France went to war over the French crown, a struggle that would last more than a century.
Then the plague came. The Black Death swept across Asia and Europe, killing perhaps a third of Europe and changing work, faith and daily life.
In 1381, English peasants rose against a poll tax and marched on London. The young king met them, but the revolt was crushed.
In Germany, a goldsmith named Johannes Gutenberg was born, the man who would change how the world made books.
Geoffrey Chaucer left his Canterbury Tales unfinished at his death, a lively crowd of pilgrims telling stories in Middle English.
Joan of Arc, a peasant girl who heard voices, helped lift the siege of Orleans in 1429. Two years later she was burned at the stake.
At Agincourt in 1415, Henry the Fifth's tired army and its longbowmen beat a far larger French force in the mud.
In the Andes, Pachacuti turned a small kingdom around Cusco into an empire, and rebuilt his capital in stone.
In Mexico, three cities joined in an alliance led by Tenochtitlan, and the Aztec Empire began gathering tribute from peoples far and wide.
The Inca Empire grew into the largest in the Americas, stretching along the Andes from Ecuador to Chile.
Gutenberg's press, with its movable metal type, made books cheap, carrying new ideas across Europe faster than ever before.
High above a river valley, the Inca rulers built Machu Picchu, a mountain estate of terraces, temples and fine stone.
Inca roads, stairways and rope bridges ran across the mountains, and relay runners carried messages from one end of the empire to the other.
In 1453, after a siege of two months, the Ottoman sultan Mehmed took Constantinople. The Byzantine Empire, Rome's last heir, was gone.
Moctezuma the Second ruled the Aztecs at the height of their power, and in 1519 welcomed strangers into his city.
Francisco Pizarro, a Spanish soldier of fortune, would lead a small force into the heart of the Inca Empire.
Hernan Cortes landed in Mexico in 1519 with a few hundred Spaniards, and found many Indigenous allies eager to throw off Aztec rule.
Cuauhtemoc, the last Aztec emperor, defended Tenochtitlan to the end, and was captured in 1521.
In Peru, Atahualpa had just won a civil war when Pizarro seized him at Cajamarca, took a great ransom, and executed him.
With their allies, and helped by disease, the Spanish took Tenochtitlan in 1521, and Mexico City rose over its ruins.
In the Andes the conquest dragged on for forty years, until the last Inca stronghold fell in 1572.
Yet the old stories survived. The K'iche' Maya wrote down the Popol Vuh, telling how the gods made the first people out of maize.
By then a new age had dawned, and the medieval world, east and west, had passed into history.
